overview:
Moldova is a small landlocked country in Eastern Europe, wedged between Romania and Ukraine, about the size of Maryland. Its gently rolling hills are covered in vineyards, orchards, and sunflower fields, and wine is so central to life that the country has some of the largest wine cellars on Earth, whole underground cities of tunnels. The capital, Chișinău, is a leafy city of parks and Soviet-era apartment blocks in the center of the country.

About 2.5 million people live in Moldova, and the number has been falling as many work abroad. The official language is Romanian, which the constitution long called Moldovan; Russian, Ukrainian, and Gagauz are also widely spoken. Most people are Orthodox Christian. Moldova is a parliamentary republic and one of the poorest countries in Europe, and its eastern strip along the Dniester River, called Transnistria, has been run by a separatist government backed by Russia since a short war in 1992, though no country recognizes it. Moldova became a candidate to join the European Union in 2022.
landAndNature: Moldova lies between two rivers: the Prut on the western border with Romania and the Dniester in the east. Between them stretches a plateau of low hills, nowhere higher than 430 meters at Bălănești, cut by wooded valleys and dotted with villages. The soil is a rich black earth ideal for grapes, wheat, corn, and sunflowers, and forests of oak and beech cover about a tenth of the country, mainly in the central Codri hills. The Orheiul Vechi gorge holds cave monasteries carved into limestone cliffs above a looping river. In the south the land opens into dry steppe near the Black Sea, which Moldova touches only through a tiny stretch of Danube riverbank. Winters are cold, summers hot, and storks, deer, and wild boar are common sights.
peopleAndCulture: Moldovans share language and many traditions with Romanians but have their own flavor. Meals include mămăligă, a golden cornmeal porridge served with sheep cheese and sour cream, plăcinte pastries stuffed with cabbage, cheese, or pumpkin, sarmale cabbage rolls, and zeamă, a chicken noodle soup. Nearly every village family makes its own wine, and the National Wine Day in October draws crowds to Chișinău. Folk music with violins, accordions, and the pan flute called the nai accompanies fast circle dances such as the hora. Martisor, a red-and-white thread charm, is worn from March 1 to welcome spring. Soccer, wrestling, and weightlifting are popular, and the Gagauz people in the south keep a Turkic language and Orthodox faith.
history: The region was part of the medieval Principality of Moldavia, whose ruler Stephen the Great fought off Ottoman armies in the 1400s and built dozens of churches. In 1812 the Russian Empire took the eastern half, called Bessarabia, and after World War I it joined Romania. The Soviet Union seized it in 1940, made it the Moldavian Soviet Republic, and deported tens of thousands to Siberia; a famine in 1946 and 1947 killed many more. Moldova declared independence on August 27, 1991. Fighting broke out in 1992 when Transnistria, with Russian support, broke away, and that dispute remains frozen. Moldova has swung between pro-Russian and pro-European governments and, after Russia invaded neighboring Ukraine in 2022, moved firmly toward the European Union, which accepted it as a candidate that year.
funFacts: The Mileștii Mici winery holds the largest wine collection in the world, nearly two million bottles stored in 200 kilometers of tunnels.
Moldovans drink more alcohol per person than almost any nation, mostly homemade wine shared with guests.
Cricova's cellars are so vast that visitors tour them by car, and streets underground are named after grape varieties.
The Gagauz people of southern Moldova speak a Turkic language but are Orthodox Christians, a rare combination.
Moldova's flag is almost identical to Romania's, differing only by the coat of arms with an eagle in the center.
